name: Phenylephrine eye gel

lead: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that constricts blood vessels. In the eye it is best known as a pupil-dilating drop used in eye examinations, and it is sold in some places in products for eye redness.

The appearance link is that narrowing visible surface vessels can make eyes look whiter and less irritated, and the same mechanism is the basis of the phenylephrine test used in eyelid (ptosis) assessment.

paras: Reported uses are as drops or gels applied to the eye surface. Clinicians use stronger drops in exams.

Wikipedia lists headache, restlessness, arrhythmias and, rarely, stroke as systemic effects, hypertensive crises with eye drops in hypertensive patients, and narrow-angle glaucoma as a contraindication; allergic reaction to phenylephrine is reported in clinical literature [1][2].

angle.text: By narrowing blood vessels on the eye surface, phenylephrine reduces visible redness, making eyes look clearer for a period.

lead: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist that causes vasoconstriction, and it is not broken down by COMT, contributing to a longer duration [1]. It was introduced for medical use in 1938 [1].

Its main ophthalmic use is dilating the pupil with 2.5% or 10% drops, often with tropicamide [1]. Because vasoconstriction whitens visible surface vessels, it also appears in redness-relief type products, which is the looks-related use. In oculoplastic surgery, a phenylephrine test is used to assess eyelid position [2].

Eye-whitening drops are a familiar part of appearance routines: narrowing the small vessels on the white of the eye makes it look clearer and brighter for a period. Phenylephrine belongs to a family of vasoconstrictor agents used this way, alongside naphazoline, tetryzoline (tetrahydrozoline), oxymetazoline and brimonidine, which differ in the receptors they act on [3][4][5][6].

paras: The appearance use rests on the vasoconstrictor action: constricting vessels in the conjunctiva reduces visible redness so that eyes look whiter and less irritated. Wikipedia describes redness-relief eye drops from this drug family, for example naphazoline products sold as Clear Eyes, which narrow swollen blood vessels in the eye.[4] Phenylephrine is listed in the legal-status notes as over the counter or prescription-only depending on the product and country.[1]

Phenylephrine eye drops dilate the pupil for retinal examination, and intracameral forms have been used in cataract surgery [1][7]. It has also been injected into the anterior chamber to control intraocular bleeding during cataract and glaucoma surgery.[1]

Naphazoline is a mixed alpha-1 and alpha-2 agonist that constricts conjunctival arterioles; it was patented in 1934 and entered medical use in 1942.[4] Tetryzoline, an alpha-1 and alpha-2 agonist, was patented in 1954 and entered medical use in 1959 for reducing eye redness from minor irritants.[3]

Brimonidine, an alpha-2 agonist whose peripheral action constricts vessels, is used to reduce eye redness and is sold under the trade name Lumify; it entered medical use in 1996.[5] Oxymetazoline is sold as Visine L.R. for eye redness, and a 0.1% ophthalmic solution was approved by the FDA in July 2020 for acquired blepharoptosis under the name Upneeq.[6]

The Müller muscle (superior tarsal muscle) is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system and helps lift the upper eyelid.[8] The phenylephrine test, used in oculoplastic assessment, applies the drug and observes the eyelid response to judge suitability for surgical options; a 2018 paper revisited the test.[2] Oxymetazoline drops for acquired ptosis are believed to act on alpha receptors in the same muscle.[6][8] For people interested in how the eyes look, eyelid height is a separate matter from redness, but the same adrenergic receptors are involved.

Low-concentration drops do not meaningfully change blood pressure, but hypertensive crisis has been reported with eye drops in people with hypertension [1]. Phenylephrine is contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma and in hypertension, hyperthyroidism and heart disease, with caution advised in Raynaud syndrome, MAOI use and prostate problems.[1] A clinical article reports an allergic reaction to phenylephrine [9].

Wikipedia's tetryzoline entry describes eye drops as sometimes causing blurred vision, irritation and dilated pupils, and says tolerance can develop with prolonged use so that stopping the drug can make the eyes redder.[3] Naphazoline eye drops are listed as causing stinging, increased redness, blurred vision, mydriasis and increased intraocular pressure in some users, with continuous use not recommended without knowing the underlying cause.[4] Prolonged nasal use of phenylephrine can cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa).[1]

Persistent redness can have many causes, from conjunctivitis to conditions that need urgent care. Wikipedia lists reduced vision, a ring of redness around the cornea, corneal changes and severe pain as signs of a serious cause needing prompt attention.[10]

Phenylephrine is a full agonist at alpha-1 receptors in most tissues with weak or minimal alpha-2 and beta activity, and causes arterial and venous vasoconstriction. It does not cross the blood-brain barrier, has an elimination half-life of 2-3 hours, and is metabolised by MAO-A and MAO-B rather than COMT.[1] Chemically it is a substituted phenethylamine, the (R)-enantiomer, usually used as the hydrochloride salt.[1]

Brand names include Neo-Synephrine and Sudafed PE; its patent has expired and generics are widely available.[1] In September 2023 an FDA advisory committee unanimously found insufficient evidence that oral phenylephrine works as a nasal decongestant, and in November 2024 the FDA proposed removing it as an active ingredient in OTC nasal decongestant monograph products.[1] These actions concern oral dosing, not eye drops.

A randomised trial found thymoxamine reversed phenylephrine-induced mydriasis from 2.5% drops in 36 of 40 eyes within an hour [11]. A phase III review covers a tropicamide/phenylephrine/lidocaine intracameral injection in cataract surgery [7]. No studies were found on phenylephrine gel specifically for cosmetic eye whitening.

timeline.event: Naphazoline, a related eye-redness vasoconstrictor, is patented.[4]
Randomised trial reports thymoxamine reversal of phenylephrine-induced pupil dilation.[11]
FDA approves oxymetazoline 0.1% ophthalmic solution for acquired blepharoptosis.[6]
FDA advisory committee finds insufficient evidence for oral phenylephrine as a nasal decongestant.[1]
